summary.text: Stem cells are undifferentiated or partially differentiated cells that can change into various cell types and multiply indefinitely to make more of themselves.
Embryonic stem cells are kept in the stem-cell stage in culture, and they come from the blastocyst's inner cell mass, whose cells can become every cell type in the body.
Adult stem cells sit in niches such as bone marrow and replenish rapidly lost cell types, and in 2006 Yamanaka's team showed mature cells can be turned back into stem cells.

items.prompt: A lab finds a cell type that divides several times but cannot divide indefinitely. How do scientists usually distinguish it from a stem cell?

options.label: It is a progenitor cell
It is an embryonic stem cell
It is a pluripotent stem cell
It is a zygote

items.explain: Stem cells proliferate indefinitely, and they are usually distinguished from progenitor cells, which cannot divide indefinitely.

items.prompt: Blood and skin cells are lost constantly. What job do adult stem cells do about this?

options.label: They stop those cells from ever dividing
They replace the cell types that are lost quickly
They turn into whole new embryos when needed
They store cells for the body to use later

items.explain: Adult stem cells exist to replenish rapidly lost cell types, such as blood and skin epithelium.

items.prompt: Researchers injected bone marrow cells into irradiated mice and found spleen lumps in proportion to the number injected. What did they conclude about each lump?

options.label: Each was a tumour caused by the radiation
Each was a lump of dead marrow
Each was a clone from a single marrow cell
Each came from several fused cells

items.explain: They hypothesized, and later confirmed, that each lump was a clone arising from a single stem cell.

items.prompt: Cells of the inner cell mass eventually become all of the body's cell types. What is this ability called?

options.label: Unipotent
Multipotent
Progenitor
Pluripotent

items.explain: Cells that differentiate into all of the body's cell types are pluripotent, while multipotent or unipotent cells make only a few types or one.

items.prompt: A team takes mature fibroblasts and changes the expression of only four genes. What do they get?

options.label: Induced pluripotent stem cells
Cloned embryos
Hematopoietic stem cells
Progenitor cells

items.explain: Yamanaka's team converted fibroblasts into pluripotent stem cells, called iPS cells, in 2006.

items.prompt: Why has isolating human embryonic stem cells been controversial?

options.label: It requires donors to give up bone marrow
It typically results in the destruction of the embryo
It can be done only in mice and not humans
It always produces cells that cannot divide

items.explain: The isolation process typically destroys the embryo, which is why sources have been restricted in some places.

paragraphs.heading: What a stem cell is
paragraphs.text: In organisms made of many cells, stem cells are cells that are undifferentiated or only partly differentiated. They can turn into various other cell types, and they can keep dividing without end to make more stem cells like themselves. They are the earliest cell in a cell lineage, and they exist in both embryos and adults, with slightly different properties in each. They are set apart from progenitor cells, which cannot divide forever, and from precursor or blast cells, which are usually committed to becoming one cell type.

paragraphs.heading: Two defining properties
paragraphs.text: Two properties mark a stem cell. Self-renewal is the ability to grow and divide over many cycles, known as cell proliferation, while staying undifferentiated. Potency is the capacity to become specialized cell types. Strictly, that means being totipotent or pluripotent, able to produce any mature cell type. Even so, progenitor cells that are only multipotent or unipotent sometimes get the name stem cell too.

paragraphs.heading: Embryonic stem cells
paragraphs.text: In mammals, the inner cell mass of the blastocyst, around days 5 to 14 of development, holds roughly 50 to 150 cells that can act as stem cells. Inside the body these cells eventually become every cell type, which is what pluripotent means. This begins at gastrulation, when they form the three germ layers: the ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. If they are removed and grown in vitro, they can be held in the stem-cell stage, and they are then called embryonic stem cells (ESCs).

paragraphs.heading: Adult stem cells
paragraphs.text: Adult stem cells live in a few chosen places in the body, called niches, such as the bone marrow or the gonads. Their job is to replace cell types that are lost quickly. They are multipotent or unipotent, so they can become only a few cell types or a single one. In mammals they include hematopoietic stem cells, which renew blood and immune cells, basal cells that maintain the skin epithelium, and mesenchymal stem cells that maintain bone, cartilage, muscle and fat cells. They are a small minority, far outnumbered by the cells they give rise to.

paragraphs.heading: Lumps in a mouse spleen
paragraphs.text: Ernest McCulloch and James Till first defined the key properties of a stem cell in the early 1960s, working at the Ontario Cancer Institute and the University of Toronto. They injected bone marrow cells into irradiated mice and found lumps in the spleens, and the number of lumps rose in a straight line with the number of cells injected. They proposed that each lump was a clone grown from one marrow cell. With Andrew John Becker and Louis Siminovitch they confirmed this, publishing in Nature in 1963, and work led by Siminovitch that year showed the colony-forming cells could renew themselves. Through this work in mice they discovered the hematopoietic stem cell (HSC).

paragraphs.heading: From the lab to the clinic
paragraphs.text: The first therapy with stem cells was a bone marrow transplant by French oncologist Georges Mathé, given to five workers at the Vinča Nuclear Institute in Yugoslavia after a criticality accident. As of 2016, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation was the only established medical therapy using stem cells. American biologist James Thomson first isolated human embryonic stem cells by 1998, but isolating them usually destroys the embryo, which has made the work controversial. In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka's team in Kyoto turned fibroblasts into pluripotent stem cells by changing the expression of just four genes, the start of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
